title: Do AI language models 'understand' the real world? On a basic level, they do, a new study finds
blurb: Michael Lepori and colleagues probe how language models represent plausible, impossible, and nonsensical events. Their analysis finds internal patterns that track human judgments, offering evidence of basic understanding of real-world situations.
displayTitle: Do language models understand the real world?

title: Study: Electrical stimulation can restore ability to move limbs, receive sensory feedback after spinal cord injury
blurb: Electrical stimulation restored muscle control and sensory feedback in three trial participants with complete spinal cord injuries. Thomas Serre contributed machine learning methods to optimize stimulation for the Intelligent Spine Interface collaboration.
displayTitle: Restoring movement and sensation after spinal cord injury

title: AI foundation models may revolutionize neuroscience, Brown researchers say
blurb: Thomas Serre and Ellie Pavlick examine how foundation models could help explain the brain. The Brown Daily Herald covers their work on prediction, digital twins, and understanding the mechanisms behind AI models.
displayTitle: What foundation models could bring to neuroscience

title: Brown University offers cash incentive to assist with 'Click Me' AI research
blurb: NBC 10 features ClickMe, the lab’s online game for collecting information about human vision. Players can earn cash prizes while helping researchers train artificial intelligence to recognize images more like people do.
displayTitle: Playing ClickMe to help train visual AI

title: Brown University to lead national institute focused on intuitive, trustworthy AI assistants
blurb: Brown leads ARIA, a $20 million NSF research institute developing AI assistants that understand people and their contexts. Thomas Serre joins a team exploring applications that include mental and behavioral health.
displayTitle: Brown to lead institute for trustworthy AI assistants

title: Inside ClickMe: Professor Thomas Serre and Jay Gopal on advancing explainable AI
blurb: Thomas Serre and Jay Gopal discuss the ideas behind ClickMe and the challenges of building human-aligned vision models. The game records which parts of images people consider important for recognizing objects.
displayTitle: Inside ClickMe with Thomas Serre and Jay Gopal

title: Explainable AI busts open black boxes
blurb: The Carney Institute profiles the Serre Lab’s research on explainability. The team develops tools to examine deep learning models and reveal which visual features contribute to the decisions those models make.
displayTitle: Opening the black box of visual AI

title: Training AI to see more like humans
blurb: The National Science Foundation features ClickMe and the lab’s work on human–AI alignment. Human annotations help train vision models to attend to the image features people use when recognizing what they see.
displayTitle: Training AI to see more like humans

title: New tool explains how AI 'sees' images and why it might mistake an astronaut for a shovel
blurb: Brown researchers introduce CRAFT, a tool for identifying the concepts a vision model uses and their importance to its decisions. The approach helps explain errors, including confusing an astronaut with a shovel.
displayTitle: CRAFT reveals the concepts behind visual AI decisions

title: Summers are for science: A look at what Brown researchers were up to this summer
blurb: The Brown Daily Herald surveys summer research at Brown, including the Serre Lab’s CRAFT project. The tool helps researchers examine how visual AI systems recognize images and why they sometimes make mistakes.
displayTitle: A summer of research into how AI sees

title: Finding the art in artificial intelligence
blurb: Thomas Serre and RISD’s Clement Valla bring neural networks into design workshops. Students and lab members explore creative applications, including blending typefaces and generating furniture designs from models of existing objects.
displayTitle: Neural networks meet art and design at RISD

title: Brain science blooms at Brown
blurb: The Brown Daily Herald explores the Carney Institute’s interdisciplinary research community. Scientists from 23 departments work together on the nervous system, with projects spanning engineering, biology, psychology, medicine, and computer science.
displayTitle: Brain science brings disciplines together at Brown

title: Carney Institute settles in above Brown bookstore
blurb: The Carney Institute moves above Brown’s bookstore at 164 Angell Street. The new offices, meeting rooms, and shared spaces support collaboration among researchers studying the brain across departments and scientific disciplines.
displayTitle: A new home for the Carney Institute

title: Intel and Brown University researchers embark on two-year project to bridge spinal cord breaks using AI
blurb: Brown, Rhode Island Hospital, Intel, and Micro-Leads Medical collaborate on an Intelligent Spine Interface. The DARPA-funded project explores how AI and neural interfaces could help restore functions lost after spinal cord injury.
displayTitle: Brown and Intel develop an intelligent spinal interface

title: Brown researchers teach computers to see optical illusions
blurb: Brown researchers build a neural network that responds to optical illusions in ways similar to people. The model offers a way to investigate visual processing while informing the design of artificial vision.
displayTitle: Teaching a computer model to see optical illusions

title: Focus on early stage of illness may be key to treating ALS, study suggests
blurb: Researchers find that inhibitory neurons are lost early in the development of ALS. The study highlights changes near the onset of disease that could matter for understanding its progression and possible treatments.
displayTitle: Early changes in ALS point to treatment questions

title: Research identifies key weakness in modern computer vision systems
blurb: Brown researchers investigate why computer vision systems struggle to judge whether two things are the same or different. Their findings expose limitations in visual reasoning and point toward questions for future models.
displayTitle: Why visual AI struggles with same–different judgments

title: University conference explores future of artificial intelligence
blurb: The Brown Daily Herald covers an interdisciplinary workshop on the future of artificial intelligence. Faculty and students from different fields gather to discuss the research questions and ideas shaping the next generation of AI.
displayTitle: A Brown workshop explores the future of AI

title: Researchers gather at Brown to discuss next-generation artificial intelligence
blurb: A workshop series at Brown brings researchers together to consider the future of artificial intelligence. The discussions examine where the field could go after the advances made possible by deep learning.
displayTitle: Researchers discuss what comes next after deep learning

title: TDP-43 Mouse Model Research Featured
blurb: The lab’s automated behavioral analysis methods help detect early changes in mice carrying a TDP-43 mutation. The Nature Neuroscience study uses machine vision to measure subtle phenotypes relevant to ALS research.
displayTitle: Measuring early behavioral changes in an ALS model

title: Artificial intelligence helps scientists map behavior in the fruit fly brain
blurb: Researchers use automated video analysis to annotate behavior in hundreds of thousands of fruit flies. The resulting maps connect actions such as walking and grooming to regions of the fly brain.
displayTitle: Mapping fruit fly behavior with artificial intelligence

title: Linking two labs a learning opportunity for Ph.D. student
blurb: Graduate student Aaron Held works across two Brown laboratories studying ALS. His research connects their expertise and provides opportunities to learn new experimental skills while investigating the disease from different scientific perspectives.
displayTitle: Learning across two labs to study ALS

title: A computer with a great eye is about to transform botany
blurb: WIRED profiles Peter Wilf and Thomas Serre’s collaboration on leaf classification. Their system learns visual patterns from thousands of leaf images, helping researchers identify plant families and investigate relationships among living and fossil plants.
displayTitle: Computer vision offers a new tool for botany

title: Meeting of the minds leads to brain science technology venture
blurb: Brown graduates explore commercial uses for software developed by Thomas Serre, Kevin Bath, and colleagues. The Neurocurious venture builds on computer vision methods that automate the observation of laboratory animal behavior.
displayTitle: Turning animal-behavior research into a technology venture

title: Computer vision can help classify leaves
blurb: Brown researchers use computer vision to classify leaves by their vein patterns. By learning from examples, the system helps assign specimens to plant families and orders, supporting a difficult task in botany.
displayTitle: Learning to classify leaves from their vein patterns

title: In analyzing a scene, we make the easiest judgments first
blurb: A Brown study finds that people make easier visual distinctions faster, challenging a fixed order for scene categorization. Computational models help researchers separate the difficulty of a judgment from its level of abstraction.
displayTitle: When judging a scene, easier distinctions come first

title: Future watch: understanding the brain
blurb: Logan Kugler’s PCMag feature examines the challenge of understanding the brain. It appears in the lab’s archive of early coverage of neuroscience and computing in the technology press.
displayTitle: Future watch: understanding the brain

title: Reverse engineering the brain
blurb: Biomedical Computation Review examines efforts to understand the brain through computational models. Roberta Friedman’s cover story includes Thomas Serre among the researchers studying how neural mechanisms give rise to intelligent behavior.
displayTitle: Reverse engineering the brain’s computational mechanisms

title: Visions of the Future - BBC Documentary
blurb: Thomas Serre’s doctoral research appears in the BBC series Visions of the Future, presented by Michio Kaku. The documentary explores artificial intelligence and the possibility of building computers inspired by the brain.
displayTitle: Brain-inspired computing in BBC’s Visions of the Future

title: Computer vision inspired by the human brain
blurb: Scientific American examines MIT research connecting neuroscience and computer vision. Models inspired by the visual system help recognize objects in complex scenes and offer a way to investigate how human vision works.
displayTitle: Teaching computers to see through models of vision

title: Easy on the eyes
blurb: The Economist covers Thomas Serre and Tomaso Poggio’s work on biologically inspired computer vision. Their model approaches human performance on rapid recognition tasks, linking theories of visual processing with machine perception.
displayTitle: A vision model approaches human recognition performance

title: Biologically Inspired Vision Systems
blurb: MIT Technology Review features a computer model inspired by the human visual system. Developed by Thomas Serre and Tomaso Poggio, it recognizes objects in busy scenes, with potential applications in surveillance and sensing.
displayTitle: Building vision systems inspired by the brain

title: Computer model mimics neural processes in object recognition
blurb: MIT News reports on a model that mimics hierarchical processing in the visual system. Thomas Serre and colleagues apply the approach to recognizing objects in complex images, including street scenes and surveillance footage.
displayTitle: Modeling neural processes to recognize objects in scenes

title: Reverse-Engineering the Brain
blurb: MIT Technology Review examines how neuroscience informs artificial intelligence. Thomas Serre and Tomaso Poggio’s vision model matches human performance on a rapid animal-detection task, testing ideas about how the brain processes images.
displayTitle: Reverse engineering vision to recognize animals in images

title: Compositionality in Neural Networks
blurb: Michael Lepori discusses whether neural networks represent concepts compositionally, as theories of human cognition propose. His Carney Institute interview also introduces NeuroSurgeon, a toolkit for finding functional subnetworks within trained models.
displayTitle: Michael Lepori on compositionality in neural networks

title: Reducing Myc gene activity extends healthy lifespan in mice
blurb: A Brown-led study finds that mice with one copy of the Myc gene live longer and remain healthier than mice with two copies. The findings connect gene activity with aging and health.
displayTitle: Reduced Myc activity extends healthy lifespan in mice

title: Computer based video in behavioral studies
blurb: Thomas Serre and colleagues at MIT and Caltech develop software that recognizes mouse behaviors in video. The freely available system automates hours of observation, matching the agreement found between human annotators.
displayTitle: Automating the analysis of laboratory mouse behavior
